10-build-process.html: DRAFT. Five steps, but spend the time on step 4: elastic-package does full QA, end to end. System tests run the package for real against a mocked API (no OVH tenant needed) and against an Elastic stack, either an existing one or a Serverless project it spawns for the run. It checks that documents are indexed, fields are mapped and assets install. Because it is all command line, the same commands run unchanged in CI/CD. Close on the bottom line: everything in a single place. The package holds the inputs, pipelines, mappings, dashboards, alerts, the documentation and the tests, so one repo is the source of truth. Plant the seed for a hands-on meetup here.
11-terraform.html: DRAFT. The transition out of the AI slide and into the OVH guest spot. What to say: for the agent to build these integrations it needed three things, and OVH provides all of them. One, the OVH MCP, which exposes the API documentation to the agent. Two, access: the Terraform-defined IAM identity (we will circle back to this in a minute) and plain API keys are both available. Three, the developer hub, with guides and references. With all of that the system created the overall integration by itself, thanks to the services the OVH team brought. Then hand off to the OVH DevRel contact, who shows the Terraform provider and the developer hub live. The old Terraform code skeleton is kept as a spare slide (11a-terraform-before.html).
12-devrel-cameo.html: DRAFT. This is the OVH DevRel contact's slide: she presents OVHcloud's developer services in her own voice, she takes the time she needs, then hands back. Rehearse the hand-off. Suggested flow for her: everything in your OVHcloud account is available over one API (the hub lists thousands of operations across v1 and v2); access is a personal access token or OAuth2 with scopes, and the Terraform provider lets you define IAM identities and policies as code (this is the circle-back from the previous slide); there are SDKs for Python, Go and Node.js plus the OKMS SDK and the ovhcloud CLI; an MCP server lets an agent talk to OVHcloud in plain language; the hub has a copy-paste prompt for your favorite AI agent (Claude, Codex, Cursor, opencode) and a playground; and the developer hub is the one place for all of it. The four tiles tagged 'used by the agent' are what powered the integrations. The operation count is read from the hub page and moves over time. She is introduced at the start of the talk, so the slide carries no name or photo.

10-ai-agent-build.html: DRAFT. The AI part. Elastic publishes skills that let an AI agent do the heavy lifting of building an integration. Flow: /research-integration does a deep analysis of the vendor API (docs, auth, data formats, ECS candidates) and writes a research brief; a generated Python script calls the API to collect a real sample; /create-integration scaffolds the package (data streams, CEL, pipelines, mappings, system tests) and the kibana-dashboards skill from elastic/agent-skills builds the dashboard from the sample; elastic-package builds, checks and tests it against a stack and a mocked API. When something fails the agent reads the error, fixes it and runs again: the self-healing loop. /maintain-integration keeps it current. Honest caveats: integration-skills is in beta and agent-skills is in technical preview. Land it with the Duke Nukem line: piece of cake. The figure is a homage, not official artwork. The AI-assisted wording on the hands-on teaser and the takeaways slides is intentionally still there and can now be reviewed.
